data.title: Comfort Systems targets mid-20% same-store revenue growth in 2027 as backlog reaches $17.8B
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Comfort Systems USA (FIX) Q3 2026

Management View

  • CEO Brian Lane said results “exceed even our recent record results,” highlighting “$13.91 per share,” backlog “grew to a new high of $17.8 billion,” and “an eighth consecutive sequential backlog increase” (CEO Brian Lane).
  • Lane announced two acquisitions and shareholder returns, saying, “I’m happy to announce the acquisition of two companies on August 1. Boys Electrical… and NeoPod,” adding “we increased our quarterly dividend by $0.10 to $1 per share, and we actively purchased shares during the quarter” (CEO Lane).
  • Lane disclosed a CFO transition: “Last night, we announced Bill’s decision to retire…,” and “Julie will be promoted to CFO as Bill’s successor” (CEO Lane).
  • CFO William George framed succession and acquisition continuity, stating, “Comfort Systems will still have the best CFO in construction,” and emphasizing, “we refuse to be hurried” in M&A (Executive VP & CFO William George).
  • George reported the quarter’s headline financials: “revenue… was $3.8 billion,” “gross profit was $934 million,” “operating income… was $625 million,” and “net income… was $489 million or $13.91 per share” (Executive VP & CFO William George).
  • President Trent McKenna highlighted demand and mix, saying “technology… was 59% of our revenue,” modular was “17% of our revenue” year-to-date, and “service revenue was higher by 13% this quarter” (President Trent McKenna).

Outlook

  • Management said, “we expect continuing growth and strong results for the remainder of 2026 and 2027” (CEO Brian Lane).
  • George provided explicit growth and margin expectations: “we expect full year same-store revenue will also be in the mid-40% range,” “same-store full year 2027 revenue will grow in the mid-20% range,” and “we currently expect that 2027 gross profit margins are likely to continue in the strong ranges that we’ve achieved” (Executive VP & CFO William George).
  • On capacity investment cadence, George said, “we estimate that full year CapEx will be 4% to 5% of revenue,” and “we’re likely to continue to incur CapEx at elevated levels during the first half of 2027” (Executive VP & CFO George).
  • Compared with last quarter, management raised its 2026 same-store growth language from “mid- to high 30% range” in Q2 to “mid-40% range” in Q3, and expanded modular capacity commentary from “approximately 5 million square feet… by late summer 2027” in Q2 to “approximately 6 million square feet… by the end of 2027” in Q3 (Executive VP & CFO William George; President Trent McKenna).

Financial Results

  • George said segment growth was driven by both platforms: “Electrical segment revenue grew by 85% and mechanical revenue grew by 43%” (Executive VP & CFO William George).
  • Profitability commentary centered on stability at high levels: “gross profit percentage remained consistent… at 24.8%,” while “margins in our electrical segment slipped to 24.3%… as compared to 26.2%” last year, which he attributed to prior-year “discrete gains” (Executive VP & CFO George).
  • Cash generation and working capital were notable: “Free cash flow for the third quarter of 2026 was $806 million,” aided by “favorable collections from large technology customers” and “$166 million in income tax payments that we were able to defer” (Executive VP & CFO William George).
  • Capital returns and investment were both active: “we invested over $100 million in CapEx to expand prefabrication facilities,” and “year-to-date, we’ve returned $349 million to our shareholders, and we’ve retired approximately 212,000 shares” (Executive VP & CFO George).

Q&A

  • Adam Thalhimer, Thompson, Davis: asked about “sequential margin decline”; President McKenna said, “we carried a higher proportion of equipment and materials… equipment doesn’t carry the margin,” and CFO George added purchase accounting “adjustments were like $12 million higher… a straight hit to margins,” while also calling the quarter “definitely early in jobs” (President Trent McKenna; Executive VP & CFO William George).
  • Adam Thalhimer, Thompson, Davis: asked whether awards were from “traditional data center customers” or “new customers”; McKenna said “there are definitely new customers creeping in” and framed the constraint as “labor,” while Lane pointed to “repeat business from very sophisticated customers” (President McKenna; CEO Brian Lane).
  • Adam Bubes, Goldman Sachs: pressed on modular expansion and new customer engagement; McKenna said the “6 million… is based on our current programmatic build-outs,” and George added, “we haven’t yet reached terms where we’re willing to accept business,” citing “the ability to pay” and 5-year volume commitments for programmatic deals (President Trent McKenna; Executive VP & CFO William George).
  • Sangita Jain, KeyBanc: asked about backlog mix and duration; George said backlog is “really lumpy,” while Lane said durations are “roughly 18 to 24 months” as project size rises (Executive VP & CFO George; CEO Brian Lane).
  • Brent Thielman, Oppenheimer: asked about customer financing risk and power availability; George described evaluating counterparties and lien rights (“the right to seize the building if we don’t get paid”), and Lane said prospects typically have power “already solved,” adding, “it really hasn’t delayed anything we’re seeing yet” (Executive VP & CFO George; CEO Brian Lane).
  • Timothy Mulrooney, William Blair: asked about data center moratorium rhetoric and modular customer concentration; George said “generally no” project impacts, while Lane added, “we have not been delayed by any moratorium,” and George explained modular focus: “why would we divert from a sure thing to sort of a mystery” (Executive VP & CFO George; CEO Brian Lane).
  • Kurt Yinger, D.A. Davidson: asked whether outsized bookings pull forward demand and about capital deployment; George said there’s “no gauge” on capacity but conditions are “extremely supportive,” and on buybacks, “we typically use 15% to 20% of our free cash flow to buy shares,” plus “we will not do a deal just because we have money” (Executive VP & CFO George).

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly positive, mixing praise (“Congrats on another great quarter”) with repeated diligence on margins, backlog duration, customer financing, moratorium/power risks, and modular customer concentration (multiple analysts).
  • Management’s tone was positive and confident in demand and execution, with defensive precision on forward margin assumptions: “we do not represent that margins will go up in the future,” while maintaining conviction that business conditions remain strong (Executive VP & CFO William George).
  • Versus last quarter, management introduced a major leadership transition (CFO retirement and successor named) and spent more time on counterparty/payment scrutiny; analyst questioning intensified around financing, moratoriums, and backlog duration compared with Q2’s emphasis on modular capacity build-out and cash flow mechanics (CEO Brian Lane; Executive VP & CFO William George).

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Backlog rose to “$17.8 billion” in Q3 from “$14.1 billion” in Q2, and management framed Q3 as an “eighth consecutive sequential backlog increase,” while Q2 emphasized reaching the first “quarterly revenue… exceeded $3 billion” (CEO Brian Lane).
  • Guidance language firmed up on growth: Q2 expected 2026 same-store growth “mid- to high 30%,” while Q3 said 2026 same-store growth “mid-40%,” and added a quantified 2027 same-store view of “mid-20%” (Executive VP & CFO William George).
  • Modular expansion timeline increased: Q2 guided to “approximately 5 million square feet… by late summer 2027,” while Q3 guided to “approximately 6 million square feet of capacity by the end of 2027” (President Trent McKenna).
  • Analyst focus expanded from Q2’s cash flow and modular backlog mechanics to Q3’s margin mix drivers, backlog duration, customer financing, and regulatory rhetoric; management repeatedly returned to labor planning discipline and customer quality screens (Executive VP & CFO George; President McKenna).

Risks and Concerns

  • Labor availability was described as the limiting factor: “the governor isn’t demand, the governor is really just labor,” with management emphasizing labor planning before accepting work (President Trent McKenna).
  • Margin variability risk was tied to project mix and stage: “early in jobs,” higher “equipment and materials” mix, and acquisition-related “purchase adjustments” flowing through cost (Executive VP & CFO William George).
  • Customer/counterparty risk in modular and large projects was explicitly addressed through payment structures and selectivity: “front and center for us is the ability to pay,” including situations requiring “very special terms” (Executive VP & CFO George).
  • Political/regulatory headlines were discussed as a monitoring item; management said no observed project delays: “I don’t know a project where one of these considerations has changed its trajectory,” and “we have not been delayed by any moratorium” (Executive VP & CFO George; CEO Brian Lane).

Final Takeaway

Comfort Systems’ management tied Q3 performance to sustained technology-driven construction demand, record backlog, and continuing modular and prefabrication investment, while signaling elevated but variable margins due to mix and job stage effects. Leadership change was a central new development, with Bill George set to retire after 2026 results and Julie Shaeff named CFO successor, as management reiterated discipline on labor planning, counterparty strength, and selective acceptance of new modular programmatic relationships.

data.title: BP, Louisiana reach deal to accelerate Deepwater Horizon payments
data.description:
BP (BP) said Friday it reached an agreement with the state of Louisiana to provide an accelerated, lump-sum $350M payment to resolve claims over the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill and settle remaining coastal zone lawsuits brought by Louisiana parishes.

Louisiana had been owed $373M ‌over ⁠the next seven years, but the state will now receive a single $350M payment under the new agreement.

"We have now disposed of ​claims and settled with all ​but ⁠one of the major defendants in these coastal cases," Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry ​said.

BP (BP) said it remains a significant energy investor in the state, where it spent $590M with Louisiana vendors and paid more than $280M in royalties and property and franchise taxes in 2025.

data.title: Elme Communities faces NYSE delisting; OTC trading to begin October 26; shares crash
data.description:
• The NYSE has initiated delisting proceedings for Elme Communities’ (ELME) shares due to abnormally low selling prices.

  • The NYSE has immediately suspended trading in Elme Communities’ common shares.

  • Elme does not intend to appeal the decision, citing its previously adopted plan of sale and liquidation, making delisting likely.

  • The company expects its shares to begin over-the-counter trading under the ticker ELMES on October 26, 2026.

    ELME shares down over 96% post-market.

data.title: Gold settles below $4,000 after steepest weekly loss in nearly five months
data.description:
Gold futures fell to three-month lows and silver slumped to its lowest level in nearly a year on ‌Friday, as higher energy prices added to inflation concerns and reinforced expectations that the Federal Reserve will maintain restrictive monetary policy.

Brent crude oil closed at its highest level in six months as as Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia continued to raise concerns over further disruption to energy supplies and traders bet on renewed fighting in the Middle East after the U.S. midterm election on November 3.

The selloff in tech stocks has also led to margin calls for ​equity traders and investors, causing them to sell gold and silver assets, American Gold Exchange analyst Jim Wyckoff said in a note.

"A rising inflation backdrop along with selling pressure to cover losses in equity or bond market positions is a negative combination for gold in the short-term, even as the Fed is looking assured to keep rates unchanged at next week's FOMC meeting," MUFG's Soojin Kim wrote.

Traders broadly expect the Fed to leave interest rates unchanged at its upcoming October 27-28 meeting, but they see a 78% probability of a hike in December, according to the CME's FedWatch Tool.

Two main factors are behind gold's recent swoon, Peter Cardillo of Spartan Capital said in a note - "First, investors are raising cash; second, Russia is selling gold holdings as the war continues to leave its economy in shambles" - but "while the risk of further downside remains, we would selectively buy at these levels."

Front-month Comex gold (XAUUSD:CUR) for October delivery fell 1.3% on Friday to $3,991.10/oz, its lowest settlement value since July 16, and front-month Comex October silver (XAGUSD:CUR) slumped 1.9% to $53.711/oz, its lowest close since November 26, 2025.

For the week, gold and silver fell 4% and 5.7%, respectively.

SpaceX-related competitive pressure contributed to the slide. Peer TMUS fell 8% as well.T has fallen about 16% in the past month

data.title: Bristol, Tempus AI partnering with Pathos AI to advance neurological treatments
data.description:
• Bristol Myers Squibb (BMY) will collaborate with Pathos AI to utilize the latter's agentic AI platform, Foundry, to build a specialized, curated dataset and agentic AI capabilities for Alzheimer’s disease and other neurological ailments.
  • Also, Bristol is the lead in the AI firm's Series E financing.
  • Though the three-year deal, "BMS aims to generate deeper insights into disease progression, identify patients most likely to benefit from potential therapies and design more precise clinical trials," per a news release.
  • Tempus AI (TEM) inked a separate deal with Pathos AI to apply the former's expertise in oncology "to create a comprehensive, de-identified, longitudinal dataset from hundreds of thousands of patients with neurological conditions, designed to track outcomes over time and accelerate biological insight." 
  • Terms call for Pathos to license the data from Tempus in a five-year, $55M agreement.

The company beat consensus estimates yet still failed to reassure investors about whether current valuations leave room for further gains.

FIX closed at $1,160.86, a decline of $118.51, as volume reached approximately 1.37 million shares, roughly 3.6 times the one-month average. This added to a recent retreat, including a nearly 9% drop on Thursday.

data.title: Corcept Therapeutics plunges 20% on Genmab cancer data
data.description:
Shares of Corcept Therapeutics (CORT), a commercial-stage biopharmaceutical company focused on cortisol modulation, sank 20% on Friday. The stock dropped $21.64 to end at $85.86 with volume of roughly 2.86 million shares, a relative volume of 3.78 times the one-month average.

The slide came after Genmab reported that a phase 3 trial of its antibody-drug conjugate, rinatabart sesutecan (Rina-S), met its primary goal for platinum-resistant ovarian cancer. CORT, which markets Lifyorli (relacorilant) for platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, dropped on the news.
